seo.title: Karmic tail 9 21 12 compatibility in the destiny matrix
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 21 12 compatibility: The Hermit, The World and The Hanged Man — what the couple wants, its path and its main task, read through the Odyssey.

title: The 9-21-12 karmic tail in compatibility: a sign only two people know
short: No single person has the 9-21-12 tail. It appears only when two birth dates are added up into a couple’s matrix — and then the centre of that couple always holds the Devil, a card that never stands at the centre of a personal chart. This is the story of a shared secret. The couple wants a world of its own, closed to outside eyes, and builds one whole out of two different lives; its main task is learning to turn its view upside down, so that the secret the two share does not become a life on hold and a wall between them.

sections.h2: The 9-21-12 program in the destiny matrix: three cards, each about a secret
paragraphs: In The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Waite describes each card in his own way, but his descriptions of the three cards of this tail rest on one and the same thing — what is hidden.

On the Hermit, Waite argues with Éliphas Lévi, who linked the card to “occult isolation, as the protection of personal magnetism against admixture”. Waite calls this “one of the frivolous renderings”. The point of the card, he says, is the truth **“that the Divine Mysteries secure their own protection from those who are unprepared”**. A secret does not need to be hidden behind a wall: whoever is not ready simply will not be able to read it.
On the World: it is “the perfection and end of the Cosmos, the secret which is within it”.
On the Hanged Man: “It is a card of profound significance, but all the significance is veiled.”

Three cards, three secrets. A secret that guards itself. A secret inside a whole world. A meaning that opens to whoever looks at it differently. And Lisovskaya, describing the same energies in a couple, finds in the minus of all three a secret of another kind — the one partners hide from each other. With 9 in a couple, problems are kept quiet and pile up. With 21, secrets and illusions about the partner appear. With 12, a pretty picture is put on show for everyone, while behind the closed door life is hard.

One more clue lies in the numbers. For every couple with this tail, the couple’s values — its spiritual purpose — fall on one of two cards of the hidden: in 69% it is the Hermit again, in 31% the Moon, which Lisovskaya calls secretive even in the plus. In most such couples the Hermit stands in two places, with two different roles: at the entry to the tail it is a shared wish; in the values it is what the union exists for.

Hence the key point: the 9-21-12 tail is a story of secrets of two kinds. There is the secret that joins: a shared sign, a language of one’s own, a world of one’s own. And there are the secrets that divide: silence, illusions, a front put up for outsiders. **The couple’s task is to keep the first from turning into the second.**

sections.h2: The Odyssey, Book 23: two people in one room
paragraphs: Odysseus came back to Ithaca after twenty years — ten years of war and ten of wandering. He entered his own house not as a king: Athena had turned him into an old beggar and given him “a staff, and a miserable wallet”. He lives at home unrecognised, and when his old nurse Eurycleia knew him by his scar, he laid his hand over her mouth. Now it is all over. The suitors who spent years eating their way through his house are gone, and Eurycleia runs upstairs to tell Penelope: he is here.
Penelope comes down — and sits opposite him, by the other wall, in the light of the fire. She says nothing. Homer, in A. T. Murray’s translation, shows her heart swinging back and forth:
and now with her eyes she would look full upon his face, and now again she would fail to know him, for that he had upon him mean raiment.
Her son cannot bear it: “thy heart is ever harder than stone”. Penelope answers him with the words the whole scene grows from:
…we two shall surely know one another more certainly; for we have signs which we two alone know, signs hidden from others.

Odysseus smiles. And so that no one in the street guesses yet what has happened in the house, he orders music and dancing. Passers-by hear the noise and decide that the queen is at last celebrating a new wedding: “Cruel she was, nor had she the heart to keep the great house of her wedded husband to the end” — “so they would say, but they knew not how these things were”.

Bathed and dressed in fresh clothes, Odysseus sits down opposite his wife again, reproaches her — “the heart in her breast is of iron” — and asks for a bed to be made up for him on his own. Here Penelope makes a move worthy of him: she tells Eurycleia to carry the bed out of the bridal chamber he built himself and make it up for him outside. Odysseus explodes. Who has moved his bed? It cannot be moved: “a great token is wrought in the fashioned bed”. He built the chamber around a living olive tree — “girth it was like a pillar” — cut away its branches, trimmed the trunk from the root and made it the post of the bed. The bed is held by a root in the earth.
Penelope’s knees give way. She throws her arms around his neck:
But now, since thou hast told the clear tokens of our bed, which no mortal beside has ever seen save thee and me alone and one single handmaid…

Then Homer makes an unexpected move — more on it below. Athena holds back the dawn: “The long night she held back at the end of its course.” Husband and wife come “to the place of the couch that was theirs of old” and tell each other everything that happened in twenty years. The Alexandrian scholars Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus, according to the ancient commentaries, set the end of the Odyssey right here — at the line about the old bed. What exactly they meant is still argued over. But for them a poem about a twenty-year journey ended not with a victory but with a bed that only two people know about.

The three cards of the tail are three layers of this scene. Two people who hide and test each other: the Hermit. Two worlds of twenty years each that have to be put together into one: the World. A test turned inside out, a night held back and a view from the other’s side: the Hanged Man.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — the Hermit: two people who know how to keep silent
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya, the first point of a couple’s tail is what the couple strives for: shared wishes, agreements, a “common language”. On the site the same card also stands in another sphere, “Relationship and common language”, at the point captioned “Common language”. So the Hermit here is not one person’s solitude but a silence that two people share and understand in the same way.

In the plus it looks like this. An evening, two people reading in the same room, not a word said in an hour — and it is not a quarrel but the best time of the week. A weekend without guests is a holiday. Friends hear about the engagement or the move after the fact. Love is shown by deeds: the lamp she complained about a month ago, he has quietly fixed; he never said he was tired, and the tea is already made. The couple has a word, a gesture, a joke from the first year that no one else would understand. Every step comes slowly, from the first kiss to a shared address, and both feel calmer that way. The two learn from each other and talk a great deal — but about what matters, not about the weather.

Homer’s word for this kind of harmony is “oneness of heart”. Odysseus, still a wanderer, wishes the young Nausicaa a husband and a home and says that “nothing is greater or better than this, when man and wife dwell in a home in one accord”. Book 23 shows what the oneness of these two is made of: they are equally cautious. Odysseus hides in his own house and claps a hand over his nurse’s mouth. “Wise” Penelope led the suitors by the nose for years and now sits by the far wall. Each of the two is a Hermit, and each is testing the other.

Here begins the resistance Lisovskaya warns about at this point: the shared wish can stand in the way of the task itself. Waite’s reversed Hermit is “Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution.” All of it is in the scene, and all of it is easy to recognise in an ordinary flat. “I’m fine,” says one, and both know it isn’t so. Instead of a question there is a test: “if they loved me, they’d guess.” Each waits to see who will speak first, and the conversation never starts. Problems get stuffed into a cupboard until the door no longer shuts. From outside, such a couple looks cold, the way his mother looked to Telemachus: a stone where the heart should be. Inside are two people with the same fear of opening up before the other does.

Waite’s main idea about the Hermit works here as a hint. A secret that protects itself has no need of walls. For twenty years Odysseus’s bed stood in a house where more than a hundred strangers feasted year after year — and the sign stayed a sign. A 9-21-12 couple does not need to shut itself off from friends and family to keep what is its own: no one could read its language anyway. **It is worth guarding not from outsiders but from the couple’s own silence.**

sections.h2: Middle of the task — the World: two whole worlds in one wreath
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya, the middle of the tail has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. The site reads it as the path — what the couple does and goes through on its way from the wish to the task. This is the site’s reading, not a statement from the book.

For Waite, the World is perfection and completion; on the everyday level, success, the road, a change of place. Wen calls it “the card of synthesis”, “a complete reconciliation of the universe’s dichotomy and duality”. In the middle of a couple’s path this means one thing: putting two different experiences together into a whole so that neither swallows the other.

Odysseus’s twenty years are the sea: war, islands, monsters, other people’s houses. Penelope’s twenty years are the house: the loom, the son, more than a hundred suitors at the table. These are two whole worlds, and on the night of the return husband and wife exchange them. She tells of the house. He tells everything in order, from the Cicones to the Phaeacians: Homer retells almost the whole Odyssey in some thirty lines, “nor did sweet sleep fall upon her eyelids, till he had told all the tale”. The circle closes when each knows the other’s story whole.

The clue in the numbers: neither of the two brings the World into the middle of this tail. A couple’s middle adds up from the middles of two personal tails, and in the three combinations of personal tails that give rise to 9-21-12, neither partner has the World. It is assembled from the two partners’ middles: The Tower and The Hierophant (16 + 5), The Hanged Man and The Hermit (12 + 9), The Devil and The Lovers (15 + 6). **This couple’s World can only be made by two.** The middle is not recalculated from the outer numbers of the tail, but here the outer numbers give the same sum: the Hermit plus the Hanged Man, 9 + 12 = 21.

In the plus, the World in a couple means travellers, people brought together by a shared philosophy of life, spouses from different countries, couples where one goes away for long stretches for work and every reunion only brings them closer. Chores are split down the middle, quarrels are settled by talking and giving way, the partner is accepted whole, even on the worst days. For a 9-21-12 couple, “the whole world” need not mean other countries. It may be his work, which she has never seen, and her family, where he is still a stranger. The middle of the path is to visit the other’s world and come back with knowledge, not a verdict.

In the minus, the circle closes like a cage. For three years Penelope wove a shroud by day, and by night, “when she had let place torches by her”, she unravelled what she had woven — Groundhog Day turned into a ruse. For a couple it is identical evenings, the same quarrel to the same script, plans discussed afresh every year and never begun. Lisovskaya also describes this minus as pressure: one partner remakes the other to suit themselves, mocks their interests, cuts them off from friends and family, shuts them up within four walls, and the couple keeps splitting up and getting back together without ever leaving the circle.

And there is illusion. To the reproach about her iron heart Penelope replies: “right well do I know what manner of man thou wast, when thou wentest forth from Ithaca on thy long-oared ship.” For twenty years she has been faithful to an image, and before her stands a different man, older, who has lived through a whole world without her. A 9-21-12 couple easily loves not the person beside them but the person that partner was in their first year together, back at university, before the children. In the reversed World, Wen finds someone “consciously and knowingly in denial”: a person sees what is going on and prefers not to know. The World in the middle asks for the opposite — to learn anew, each time, who is beside you now.

sections.h2: Main task — the Hanged Man: turning the view upside down
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya, the last point of a couple’s tail is the main task, the chief problems and trials. It is read mostly through the minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn.

Lisovskaya describes the minus of energy 12 in a couple almost as Penelope’s fate. One partner holds the relationship together with all their strength, gives way, adapts — and gets reproaches in return, yet cannot leave, because keeping the family together matters more to them than anything. Penelope kept the house alone for twenty years, and the first thing she hears on the day of the return is a heart of stone from her son and a heart of iron from her husband. In a 9-21-12 couple this happens when one partner carries the household, the children, the relatives or the lack of money for years — and is told in return that they are cold.

The second minus is life put off until later. Waite writes that all the Hanged Man’s significance “is veiled”; Penelope spent three years weaving a shroud, a veil of her own, and unravelling it every night. This is what a decision that hangs for years looks like: “after the renovation”, “when the kids are grown”, “when he changes”, “when we’ve paid off the loan”. By day they weave, by night they unravel, and no one says aloud what exactly they are waiting for.

The third is the crowd. Waite’s reversed Hanged Man reads “Selfishness, the crowd, body politic.” Lisovskaya writes about couples for whom what people will say matters more, and about decisions made because “that’s how it’s done”. In the Odyssey the street passes its verdict by the sound of the music — “Cruel she was” — at the very moment when the opposite is happening inside the house. A 9-21-12 couple easily builds the right picture for the street and pays dearly for it behind the closed door.

This minus has a quiet, almost beautiful version. In O. Henry’s story “The Gift of the Magi” (1905), Della secretly sells her hair to buy Jim a chain for his watch, and Jim secretly sells his watch to buy her combs. Two secrets and two sacrifices meet — and both gifts turn out to be useless. This is the Hermit and the Hanged Man together: everything for the other, and everything kept from them. O. Henry says that “of all who give gifts these two were the wisest”, and the love in the story is real. But a 9-21-12 couple recognises itself in it by another sign: surprises nobody asked for, and sacrifices the other learns about last.

Waite insisted that the Hanged Man “has been called falsely a card of martyrdom” and a card of duty. In his description the hanging man’s face expresses **“deep entrancement, not suffering”**. The Hanged Man’s task is not to endure but to stop and see what cannot be seen from the usual position. Book 23 has three such turns.

The first is the test turned inside out. Throughout his return, Odysseus was the one doing the testing: he disguised himself, made up false names, tested everyone, even his wife. Penelope does the same to him, and the master of disguise loses his composure for the first time. Recognition comes not when the secret is kept but when the mask slips.

The second is a simile. When Penelope embraces her husband, Homer compares her joy to the joy of swimmers who have reached the shore after a shipwreck: “welcome as is the sight of land to men that swim, whose well-built ship Poseidon has smitten on the sea… even so welcome to her was her husband”. It was Odysseus who survived the shipwreck, but the epic gives this image to her: twenty years of waiting are a sea too. The classicist Helene Foley called such passages “reverse similes”, and the Odyssey has several of them. Odysseus weeps over a song about Troy as a woman weeps over her husband fallen before his city. He himself compares Penelope to a blameless king whose fame “goes up to the broad heaven”. Again and again Homer swaps the roles, so that each sees the other’s path as their own.

The third is the night held back. Athena does not let the dawn begin, and time hangs at the edge of the sky. This is suspension by choice, not from helplessness: a night in which nothing is settled except one thing — to talk it all through.

Hence the main task of a 9-21-12 couple. **Not to wait in silence, but to name what they are waiting for.** Not to sacrifice in secret, but to ask. To see the partner’s years as a voyage of their own, even if all that time the partner stayed at home. And to be able to stop time for the two of them: an evening, a trip, a night of talk when everything else can wait. Which of the pair is Odysseus and which is Penelope is not decided by sex; more often each is both.

If there is fear in the couple — one partner controls the other’s every step, keeps them from the people close to them, raises a hand to them — this is not a “task of the tail” and not something to wait out the way Penelope waited. In danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line; for the rest, see a psychologist.

sections.h2: The Devil at the centre: a bond neither partner has alone
paragraphs: In every couple with the 9-21-12 tail, the sphere “The atmosphere inside the couple”, at the centre of the matrix, holds 15 — the Devil. Yet in a personal matrix no birth date gives a centre of 15: a personal centre is 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. So **the Devil in this matrix is the one card that belongs only to “us”**. Neither of the two brings it: it arises between them.

In the plus of this energy Lisovskaya sees passion, acceptance of each other’s dark sides, powerful support, a readiness to change for the sake of love. But even in the plus one partner may wake up wanting to possess the other — hence resentment and jealousy. In the minus: control, attempts to hold on through intimacy, a child, money or status. She ends her chapter on energy 15 with the thought that nobody belongs to anybody. Waite’s description of the card leaves the same hope: he who is exalted above the chained figures “is not to be their master for ever”. And among the Devil’s divinatory meanings he lists this one: “that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”.

Next to the tail, this combination explains a great deal. The Hermit gives the couple a secret; the Devil gives the pull that holds the two inside that secret. Together they create a world no third person enters, and in the minus even the two of them find it hard to get out: a closed room where love quietly turns into surveillance. The minus of the World in the middle — isolation within four walls — sounds louder with the Devil at the centre.

But Book 23 also shows the other side of the same force. What strips off Odysseus’s mask is not cunning but an outburst: at the thought that the bed has been moved and the root cut through, for the first time all evening he speaks not with calculation but with heat. A feeling that cannot be acted is what proves to Penelope that it is him. And their bed holds the two of them not by a chain but by a root: no man, “be he never so young and strong”, could “easily pry it from its place”, yet each lies down in it of their own accord.

sections.h2: On the Waite–Smith cards: the Hanged Man and the World are one figure
paragraphs: This section is about the classic Waite–Smith deck. The cards on this site have different artwork, so there is no point looking for the details below on them.

On the Waite–Smith card the Hanged Man hangs head down, one leg bent behind the other, and his legs form a cross. The dancing figure of the World crosses her legs in exactly the same way. Wen points this out: **“Note the tau cross in the legs reemerging in Key 21: The World”** — “suggesting that it is the hanged man who shall attain the fulfillment of the World card, not the mob”.

For the 9-21-12 tail this is the key picture. The middle of the path and the main task are one and the same figure in two positions: dancing and head down. What the couple sees as a whole world in the middle of the path has to be seen upside down in the main task. And the other way round: the suspension that looks like a dead end is the same dance, only turned on its head.

Waite also has a line about the Devil that fits the couple’s centre exactly. In the old decks two small demons were tied to the Devil’s pedestal; in the Tarot of Papus, Waite writes, they were replaced by “naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other” — and “the author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism”. There people are tied not to the pedestal but to each other. That is the Devil at the centre of a 9-21-12 couple: a bond with no third end.

sections.h2: How the 9-21-12 circle closes — and how it opens
paragraphs: In the minus, the tail turns like this. Silence instead of talk (9): the two carefully leave the sore spots alone. The couple’s world shrinks to a familiar circle, and each lives with an image of the other rather than with the person (21). One starts pulling for two and waiting, decisions hang, and the right picture is kept up for the street (12). The resentment that builds up goes back into silence — and the circle starts again. From outside all is calm; inside, two people sit for years by opposite walls of one room.
What opens the circle is what Penelope and Odysseus did in a single night:

ul: **Ask in a way only the real person can answer.** Not with a trap but with a question: what do you feel now, what do you want, what has changed this year.
**Tell each other the whole world.** Regularly and in detail: what happened to each at work, with family, in their head — including what seemed not worth telling.
**Name the waiting out loud.** What exactly are we waiting for, who is waiting, and what do we do while we wait. Waiting without words turns into sacrifice.
**Retell the partner’s path in the first person.** The way Homer gives Penelope the shipwreck: see that the other was at sea too.
**Hold back the night.** Time for two, when nothing is decided and nobody hurries, is not a reward but part of life.
**Guard the couple’s own room, not secrets from each other.** A shared sign, yes; separate cupboards full of things unsaid, no.
**Leave the crowd outside the door.** The couple’s decisions are made by the two of them, not by relatives and not by “what people will say”.

paragraphs: At its strongest, this is a couple with a sign of its own. It needs no walls to stay itself: what matters most is understood only by the two of them anyway. It can live through two different worlds and put them together into one — each time learning anew who the other is now. And it can stop time: fall silent, turn its view upside down, see the other’s path — and say what for years seemed impossible to say. The secret of such a couple guards itself. Not because it is hidden, but because the only one who can read it is the one who built that bed with you on the root of a living tree.

sections.h2: How to calculate the 9-21-12 tail from two dates
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices; a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. Example: a couple born on 17.09.1994 and 21.09.1976.
First partner: day 17, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 9 + 4 = 23 → 5. Karmic task 17 + 9 + 5 = 31 → 4, centre 17 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 35 → 8. Personal tail: 12-16-4.
Second partner: day 21, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task 21 + 9 + 5 = 35 → 8, centre 21 + 9 + 5 + 8 = 43 → 7. Personal tail: 15-5-8.

paragraphs: The couple’s middle is taken from the middles of the personal tails, not calculated from the couple’s two outer numbers. Here both ways give 21, but that is not always so: in 50 of the 97 couple tails the middle does not match the sum of the outer numbers. This couple’s values are 9, the Hermit; they are recalculated from the couple’s own sums, not added up from the partners’.

sections.h2: Where 9-21-12 comes from and how common it is

ul: The 9-21-12 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 41 — 2.4%. That is 12th place among the 97 couple tails and the most common tail whose main task is 12.
It forms from only three combinations of the partners’ personal tails: 12-16-4 and 15-5-8 (51% of such couples), 9-12-3 and 18-9-9 (31%), 9-15-6 and 18-6-6 (18%).
Every such couple has 15, the Devil, at the centre. The couple’s values are 9 in 69% and 18 in 31%.

9-21-12 cannot be a personal tail. With a main task of 12, the personal centre is always 6 and the tail is 18-3-12. The Hermit at the entry would need a centre of 15 (12 + 15 = 27 → 9), and no person has such a centre.

paragraphs: The partners’ personal tails are read by their own rules. They cannot show which of the two “brings” the Hermit or the Hanged Man into the couple: the couple’s tail is shared.

sections.h2: 9-21-12 and 9-12-21: the same cards in a different order
paragraphs: The same three numbers give one more couple tail — 9-12-21 (1.9% of couples, the centre likewise always 15). In it the Hanged Man moves to the middle of the path and the World becomes the main task: there, suspension is the road, and the task is to complete and assemble a shared world without closing it into a circle. No other orderings of these numbers occur in a couple’s matrix.

ul: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; revised edition 1922): the Hermit, the Hanged Man, the Devil, the World — parts I–III.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): Key 9, Key 12, Key 15, Key 21.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple’s points; energies 9, 12, 15, 18 and 21 in a couple.
Homer, The Odyssey, translated by A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library, 1919): books 2, 6, 8, 13, 19 and 23.
Helene P. Foley, “Reverse Similes” and Sex Roles in the Odyssey, Arethusa 11 (1978).
O. Henry, “The Gift of the Magi” (1905).

**M · Entry to the task — 9, The Hermit.** What the couple wants together: a silence for two, a language of its own, signs only the two of them understand. The same wish turns into resistance when the silence starts hiding what needs to be said.

**N · Middle of the task — 21, The World.** How the couple walks its path: by putting two different experiences together into one whole. The risk is a closed circle where every day is like the last, and what lives beside each of them is not a person but a memory of one.

**D · Main task — 12, The Hanged Man.** To stop the usual course of things and look at the union from the other side. In the minus, one partner holds everything up and waits, decisions hang for years, and life is put off until “later”.

intro: This story was written long before the destiny matrix. In Book 23 of the Odyssey, a husband and wife who have not seen each other for twenty years sit in the same room and cannot recognise each other. What helps them is not a miracle but a secret known only to the two of them. Behind the three cards of the tail, this is the scene that shows through — and what follows is the evidence: what the cards themselves say, what the books say and what the numbers say.

faq.q: What does the 9-21-12 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple’s tasks, written in three cards. The Hermit at the entry: the couple wants a quiet world and a language of its own. The World in the middle: it puts two different experiences together into one whole. The Hanged Man as the main task: it has to learn to stop, to name its waiting out loud and to see the union through the partner’s eyes.

faq.q: Is the 9-21-12 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple’s tail shows what the two have to learn, not how it will all end. The Hanged Man as the main task is not a verdict and not a duty to endure, but the skill of making a pause alive and turning the view upside down. This tail occurs in roughly one couple in 41.

faq.q: Why does a couple with the 9-21-12 tail have the Devil at the centre?
faq.a: Running through every date shows that each couple with this tail has 15 at the centre. No single person has such a centre, so the Devil here is a card that only the couple has: a force of attraction and attachment that must not be allowed to turn into control.

faq.q: Can 9-21-12 occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix, with a main task of 12 the centre is always 6, and the tail comes out as 18-3-12. The order 9-21-12 occurs only in a couple’s matrix, where each point is the sum of two people’s points.

faq.q: Which partner is responsible for the Hanged Man?
faq.a: Neither on their own. The couple’s tail is shared: each of its points adds up from both partners’ numbers. The roles of the one who waits and the one who leaves, the one who tests and the one being tested often switch in such a couple, and sex does not assign them.

faq.q: What should a couple with the 9-21-12 tail do?
faq.a: Look after their common language without hiding what matters from each other; regularly tell each other what is going on in each one’s world; say out loud what they are waiting for; make no decisions for the sake of what people will say; find time when the two are simply alone together and talk things through.

report: For twenty years a husband and wife have not seen each other, and now they sit in one room by opposite walls — in silence. This is Book 23 of the Odyssey, and the whole story of the 9-21-12 couple’s tail is played out in it. What helps Penelope and Odysseus recognise each other is not a miracle but what Penelope tells her son: “we have signs which we two alone know, signs hidden from others”.

The secret here is not a pretty metaphor stretched to fit the cards. It is written into the cards themselves. Waite on the Hermit: **“the Divine Mysteries secure their own protection from those who are unprepared”**. On the World: “the perfection and end of the Cosmos, the secret which is within it”. On the Hanged Man: “all the significance is veiled”. And in the minus of the same energies in a couple, Lisovskaya finds a secret of another kind — the one partners hide from each other: silence about problems, secrets, illusions about the partner, a pretty picture for everyone else. The 9-21-12 tail is a story of secrets of two kinds: one joins, the others divide. **The couple’s task is to keep the first from turning into the second.**

report.h3: A secret that guards itself needs no walls

report: At the entry to the task stands the Hermit — what the couple wants together, its common language. In the plus it is a silence for two: an evening when not a word is said in an hour, and it is the best time of the week; a weekend without guests; love shown by deeds; a word or gesture from the first year that no one else would understand.

The Odyssey shows what the oneness of these two rests on: both are equally cautious. Odysseus hides in his own house disguised as a beggar and lays a hand over the mouth of the nurse who has recognised him. Penelope sits by the far wall and does not believe. Waite’s reversed Hermit is “Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution.” In an ordinary flat it sounds like “I’m fine” when both know it isn’t so; like a test instead of a question — “if they loved me, they’d guess”; like a conversation that never starts because each is waiting to see who will speak first.

For twenty years Odysseus’s bed stood in a house where more than a hundred strangers feasted year after year — and the sign stayed a sign. A couple with this tail does not need to shut itself off from friends and family to keep what is its own: no one could read its language anyway. It is worth guarding not from outsiders but from the couple’s own silence.

report.h3: Two whole worlds and one night to put them together

report: The middle of the path is the World, for Wen “the card of synthesis”. Odysseus’s twenty years are the sea; Penelope’s are the house. On the night of the return they exchange these worlds, “nor did sweet sleep fall upon her eyelids, till he had told all the tale”. Neither of the two brings this couple’s World: it can only be made by two. And “the whole world” need not mean other countries: it may be his work, which she has never seen, and her family, where he is still a stranger.

In the minus the circle closes like a cage: identical evenings, the same quarrel to the same script, plans discussed every year and never begun. And illusion. To the reproach about her iron heart Penelope replies: “right well do I know what manner of man thou wast, when thou wentest forth from Ithaca on thy long-oared ship.” A couple with this tail easily loves not the person beside them but the person that partner was in the first year. The World in the middle asks for the opposite — to learn anew, each time, who is beside them now.

report.h3: Twenty years of waiting are a sea too

report: The main task is the Hanged Man, and it is read through the minus. One partner holds the relationship together with all their strength and gets reproaches in return. Penelope kept the house alone for twenty years, and on the day of the return she hears from her son of a heart of stone, from her husband of a heart of iron. Decisions hang for years: “after the renovation”, “when the kids are grown”, “when he changes”. For three years Penelope wove a shroud by day and unravelled it by night.

Waite writes that the Hanged Man’s face expresses **“deep entrancement, not suffering”**. The task is not to endure but to turn the view upside down, and Book 23 has three such turns. Penelope tests the great tester by his own method, ordering the bed carried out of the bridal chamber — and the master of disguise loses his composure for the first time: “a great token is wrought in the fashioned bed”. The chamber is built around a living olive tree, and the bed is held by its root. When Penelope embraces her husband, Homer compares her joy to that of swimmers who reach the shore after a shipwreck. It was Odysseus who survived the shipwreck, but the epic gives this image to her: twenty years of waiting are a sea too. And finally, Athena holds back the dawn: a night in which nothing is settled except one thing — to talk it all through.

Hence the key point for a couple with this tail: **not to wait in silence, but to name what they are waiting for**. Not to sacrifice in secret, but to ask. To see the partner’s years as a voyage of their own, even if all that time the partner stayed at home. Which of the pair is Odysseus and which is Penelope is not decided by sex; more often each is both.

report.h3: A bond with no third end

report: At the centre of every couple with this tail stands the Devil, and no one has such a centre in a personal chart. It is the one card that belongs only to “us”. Waite describes the Tarot of Papus, where the Devil’s figures are human beings “yoked only to each other”, and praises the symbolism. The Hermit gives the couple a secret; the Devil gives the force that holds the two inside it. In the minus the closed room turns into surveillance, and then Lisovskaya’s conclusion is worth remembering: nobody belongs to anybody. If there is fear in the couple — one partner controls the other’s every step, keeps them from the people close to them, raises a hand to them — this is not a task of the tail and not something to wait out: in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line; for the rest, a psychologist.
But the same force strips off masks. What gives Odysseus away is not cunning but a burst of feeling that cannot be acted. And their bed holds the two not by a chain but by a root.

At its strongest, a 9-21-12 couple is two people with a sign of their own who need no walls to stay themselves. They can live through two worlds and put them together into one, they can stop time and turn their view upside down. **Their secret guards itself**: not because it is hidden, but because only those who built that bed together can read it.
